speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: asked the Minister for Education what additional measures are being considered to address the high stress levels reported by teachers in the recent OECD TALIS 2024 study, particularly regarding support for their mental health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: My response will also cover related oral and written Parliamentary Questions set down for today and subsequent Sittings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A teacher's responsibility is significant, as it involves nurturing students and shaping their futures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our teachers take great pride in their work and demonstrate a strong sense of professionalism and dedication.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our educators often go far beyond their formal duties because they see their students' growth and well-being as their responsibility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we appreciate and applaud their passion, we also want to ensure that such commitment does not result in unsustainable workload for our teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members asked about the teachers' role and how the Ministry intends to support teachers with their non-teaching workload.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members also asked about the use of independent or externally verified studies to validate reported teacher workload hours and if the Ministry conducts regular checks of teacher workload.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We recognise that teaching, like many professions, comes with its own set of challenges and stressors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These longer hours are reported because Singapore teachers spend their time differently from many of their OECD peers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While classroom teaching hours are shorter, our teachers spend time on other important activities such as lesson preparation, co-curricular activities (CCAs) and professional development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These activities are critical to their effectiveness in providing holistic education for our students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: TALIS, being the largest international teacher survey, is a useful benchmarking tool, but it has its limitations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is conducted once every six years and surveys a representative sample of only our lower-secondary teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In contrast, the Ministry of Education (MOE) internally monitors the workload of our teachers more regularly – across all grade levels: primary, secondary, junior college and centralised institute – through surveys, polls and various forms of staff engagement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This allows us to track closely and develop a more holistic understanding of teacher workload trends and issues, so that we can adjust our policies and programmes, as necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, we recognise that the complexity of a teacher's work has increased over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members asked how MOE aims to address the longer working hours and stresses faced by our teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MOE adopts a range of measures to manage teachers' workload and to support their well-being, which we review regularly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, MOE's Teacher Work Management Framework provides our school leaders with a common set of principles and measures to guide equitable workload allocation, considering teachers' competencies and preferences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It emphasises transparency, trust and open communication in workload deployment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is reviewed regularly in response to new developments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MOE is tapping on AI to help teachers work more efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Digital platforms, like Parents Gateway, have reduced time spent on administrative tasks, such as collecting consent forms and medical certificates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And while Singapore has one of the highest adoption rates among OECD education systems for using AI, we recognise that it does not immediately translate to reduced work hours.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Teachers need time to be trained to use these tools, be comfortable using them and to fully integrate these tools into their work practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On average, each school has about 85 teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, each school is resourced with a team of allied educators performing functions, such as counselling and working with students with special educational needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All schools have a dedicated administrative team overseeing general administrative matters, procurement, financial operations and logistics support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Furthermore, schools have the flexibility to procure manpower services such as coaches, CCA administrators and allied support for student well-being; as well as vendors to assist with administrative work, events management and student programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to review the number of non-teaching staff needed in schools to effectively support our teachers and our students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When we introduce new policies and initiatives, or make policy changes, it increases workload for a season, as schools and teachers need to be briefed, trained and need time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MOE has given schools greater flexibility to pace the implementation of new system-wide initiatives, including deferring them if necessary, in order to manage staff workload.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, schools could decide when they would implement major changes, such as Full Subject-Based Banding as well as the EdTech Masterplan 2030.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All schools provide protected vacation time during school holidays to ensure that our teachers can rest and recharge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It also states clearly that teachers do not need to give their personal mobile phone numbers to parents and students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is to minimise the blurring of lines between work and personal time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since 2022, MOE has also provided guidelines on FWA for School-based Officers, while maintaining the duty of care towards our students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include allowing teachers to report later at the start of the school day or leaving earlier before the end of the school day if they have no lessons or duties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Teachers are also allowed to work from home on a day where they have no classes or duties requiring their presence in school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Teachers who are unable to take on the full workload can apply for part-time working arrangements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All schools have Staff Well-being Committees that are resourced with Staff Welfare Funds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Teachers have access to a range of resources such as well-being workshops, talks, webinars and online self-care materials.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If they have well-being concerns, they are encouraged to raise them with their supervisors, school leaders or superintendents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They also have access to peer support, such as their school's wellness ambassadors and to free professional counselling through MOE's in-house counsellors or the whole-of-Government Employee Wellness Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members asked if the reduction of workload will be a key priority with key performance indicators set, and how well-being data informs staffing, performance evaluation and retention policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MOE takes a holistic approach to monitoring teacher well-being rather than using singular metrics like work hours.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We regularly track a range of indicators including job satisfaction, retention rates and stress levels and also, engage with MOE teachers' unions to get feedback and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This approach allows us to ensure timely interventions to support teacher well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Apart from broad-based measures to support the profession, when we receive school-specific feedback, we will also implement targeted measures to address these issues in those schools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are encouraged by the commitment shown by our teachers over the years, in spite of the growing complexity of the role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Based on the results from MOE's staff engagement survey last year, teachers' perceptions of work-life balance support were comparable to those across the wider Public Service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, our individual and collective attitude towards educators will determine whether we can continue to attract and retain good educators.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond MOE and our schools, parents and other stakeholders also play an important role in supporting our teachers' well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By working collaboratively with schools, respecting educators and maintaining realistic expectations about the responsibilities of teachers, parents can also help create an environment where our teachers can focus on what they do best – educating and nurturing our children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a society, let us cherish our educators' contributions each and every day.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For when we honour those who teach our children, we strengthen the foundation upon which our nation's progress rests.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I thank all parents and members of the public for your support for our schools and our teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We appreciate our teachers and we are committed to working with you to nurture and guide our next generation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: So, I want to first appreciate the Minister for sharing the efforts taken by the Ministry to protect our teachers, for their well-being, and of course, how they have been treated in schools all this while.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: I have gotten a number of on-the-ground feedback, including those with dialogues through the Singapore Teachers' Union (STU), where I am an advisor for, and we have had very good conversations about how we want to improve teachers' well-being and how we can protect them further.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And while many support and welcome the efforts done by the Ministry, one pain point that keeps cropping up is the workload.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And we have heard from Minister on how we have continued to monitor.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: But they have shared progressively that, although things have changed, it is similar still, because you move the pieces around, but the plate is still as much.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: So, there are some concerns, and I would like to ask further.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The Minister talked earlier about how he has done some research and we know OECD's survey is not ours, but we have continually done more, to check on our teachers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The Minister also mentioned the use of AI, which I believe has helped teachers a lot, but it has also added a layer of complexity to how they do things.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And I wonder whether this could also be considered in us trying to reduce the workload.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: The Minister mentioned earlier, they teach a certain amount of hours, but it is the bulk of whatever happens after that, that is the one that really needs some protection.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: And I hope that the Minister could find some model to help them in that regard.
I think the STU has certain considerations too, so I think it is wonderful if we can work further on this.
And the Minister mentioned earlier how we have decentralised, such that different schools will have different approaches.
I think that is necessary, given the demographics of the different schools.
But would you consider in this regard certain schools with slightly different needs?
For example, they have a higher number of need for counselling, they need more para educators to be on board.
So, I thank the Minister again, for sharing the efforts in protecting teachers' well-being and I want to appreciate the teachers too.
We are coming towards the end of the year and I want to appreciate the good work they have done over the whole year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, as I said, we do not just rely on TALIS, which is an OECD study.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I mentioned that over the years we have moved some responsibilities away from teachers towards allied educators, like counsellors, special educational needs (SEN) officers, administrators, vendors and others.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have given schools resources to be able to bring in more vendors, if necessary, to help them to organise the activities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, those are the measures that are in response to a deeper understanding of the issues that the teachers face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we are committed to continue this work and continue to implement new measures to help to allow our teachers that space to teach.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would say that teaching today, if you ask any teacher, is a lot more holistic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not just about in-classroom teaching of a core subject or a hard subject.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even in the teaching of a hard subject, I think the Member will recognise that we are infusing 21st Century Competencies through the way that the teaching is carried out – through field trips, through studies, in subjects where appropriate, we infuse even values education, and Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) into some of these subjects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, teaching being more holistic, is no longer just found in the classroom, but also in CCA and CCE, and in a whole range of other activities that enable our teachers to mould and nurture our students holistically – not just cognitively, but affectively, in terms of their emotional well-being, in terms of their skillsets, in terms of their executive functioning, in terms of their core values that help them to navigate society and the uncertain future world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And of course, by helping our teachers with tools to prepare their material – standardised material in SLS – so they do not always have to prepare their own material, they can use some of that and adjust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also provide AI tools, not just administratively to help them with administrative workload, but also to help them augment their teaching, augment their marking, augment their ability to give feedback to their students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I just want to refer the Member back again to the various measures I articulated earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Member asked whether we give our schools more resources based on needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There was a Parliamentary Question sometime back where Members asked if schools can get more allied educators based on the profile of their students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, if they need more SEN officers or more counsellors, we are able to redeploy the existing pool and steer them towards schools that may have a greater need, whether secular or for a season.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am only going to call Members who have filed questions on this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, for those who did not, you do not need to raise your hands.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: My supplementary questions will be shorter than Dr Wan Rizal's.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: It is a common refrain from many teachers that one hour in the classroom is more tiring than one hour in the office.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: I would venture to extend that to say that one hour in the classroom is much more tiring than one hour in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: So, we should all be rightfully concerned about our teachers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: To that end, I have two supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: So, my question to the Minister is whether the low proportion is a feature of MOE's hiring policy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Is it because it is about low recruitment or is it about high attrition?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: And if it is the latter, what is the Ministry doing about it?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: The second and last question is about non-teaching workload.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: I fully agree with the Minister that non-teaching workload that leads to educational outcomes are important.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Our teachers should do that, like for CCAs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Because teachers do not just teach, they educate.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: But there are also non-teaching workloads that do not necessarily lead directly to educational outcomes – procurement, for example, and other administrative work.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: It seems like a perennial bugbear, notwithstanding the Minister's assurance, that the amount of resources to each school has gone up.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Is it because the workload has gone up more than the resources given to the schools?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I said earlier in my speech that both TALIS, as well as our surveys show that while teachers' workload is high – it is indeed so and working hours are long – they have been stable over the past number of years, and we are working hard to focus our teachers' precious time on teaching holistically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where possible, we help them to be more productive and effective, help them to shed some of the administrative tasks and what the Member calls, non-core teaching functions to allied educators and others.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, why is it that the number of working hours remains at this level and remain stable over the past number of years?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think Members will also need to look at the context.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the past few years, we have made a number of policy changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Teaching, as I said today, is a lot more holistic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is a lot more teaching beyond the classroom.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is CCA, through which we teach leadership, sportsmanship, empathy and so on, the 21st Century Competencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in short, we have made many education-related moves over the years to strengthen our education system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, Full Subject-Based Banding only recently kicked in and there are a lot of things to be done in order to allow our students at secondary level to be able to learn at their pace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, it creates more work, but one which teachers recognise benefits our students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We implemented an EdTech Masterplan 2030 to help support our teachers and our students in learning using technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not just learning using technology, but learning with technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have been talking about AI in education as well, so that will of course, create additional workload in terms of briefing, understanding, tinkering, learning, workshopping, practising, mastering and then we start to reap the results.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That, of course, creates additional work, but again for a purpose that supports the education system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We made changes to refresh our 21st Century Competencies and how it is infused into our lesson plans and in our curriculum and in holistic education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That, of course, also requires all our schools, all our teachers and all our departments, not just in the headquarters (HQ), but particularly in our schools, to make changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I can go on and on about all these things that have been done over the last few years that will increase the workload for a season, or some may also increase workload secularly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because education is more holistic and our teachers also have to contend with a changing demographic of parents and the different aspirations of our students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, all in, being able to keep workload at that level, despite doing all these important things, I think is a reflection of how these measures have worked.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we need to do more in order to make further improvements to the workload and stress on our teachers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On beginning teachers, the Member asked why the proportion of beginning teachers has fallen through the TALIS report; he cites that.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Has the Ministry actively conducted studies on other countries on how they manage this topic of time management for teachers?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If so, which countries are they, and have there been anything that is implemented in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The second question is, what targeted initiatives are there being planned to reduce teacher attrition rates, particularly among our younger educators who may feel overwhelmed by workload and pressure?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through TALIS, we have a very useful comprehensive teacher survey study across a large number of OECD countries and that is a very useful benchmarking tool.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not just survey results, but they also go into some qualitative understanding of each jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That, of course, complements our comparative study of other jurisdictions to continually improve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, that is the response to her first question.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I mentioned quite a number of them earlier, for example, coming to school a little later, if there is nothing right up in the morning, leaving once their teaching and other duties are done, and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we will continue to find ways to make sure that our scheme of service continues to respond to a changing demographic.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The TALIS findings underscore our Singapore teaching profession as innovative and respected, yet burdened by the demands that could potentially erode long-term sustainability, particularly our early career educators.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this aspect, I have three supplementary questions for the Minister.
First, do teachers appraisal and progression factor in non-teaching duties, such as projects and CCAs?

The second supplementary question concerns whether the Ministry has sought teachers' feedback on the demands that they face from students' parents and whether the situation has improved with the introduction of the Parents Gateway communication platform, as shared by the Minister earlier?

And finally, I am not sure if I caught it, in the various measures that the Minister shared earlier, in relation to supporting the young, budding teachers, whether we are prepared to consider to include a scheme like a mentorship between senior and more junior teachers, as a form of buddy system, encouraging and providing the necessary support and guidance to the young educators?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think I will address the Member's third question first.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I did mention earlier that mentoring, on top of induction programmes and other professional development programmes, are in place for beginning teachers – or what she mentions as novice teachers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Kenneth Tiong, I know you have filed a Parliamentary Question for this tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Surely, the Ministry must have a direction or goals, whether it is fewer hours, better allocation of time from administrative duties to teaching, or something else.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Without that, how do we measure whether AI adoption is achieving the desired outcomes?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The second supplementary question: the Minister said that the workload has been stable at 53 hours per week.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Does MOE believe that this is sustainable in the long term?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And if not, what is the target number of hours that MOE is working towards?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I mentioned earlier that AI tools, once you introduce them, there is work created when you introduce AI tools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, there is work created when you introduce any productivity tool.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the NIE70 conference, we also had AI experts from abroad who cautioned that when you introduce AI tools, there is hidden work that is created.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But if these are tools that are productive in nature that help save effort, reduce time spent on certain things in order for the teacher or the worker to be able to do more higher value-added things and divert the time to things that they feel are more important, then the necessary pre-condition is that one gets familiar, understands and then gradually masters and gets familiar with the tools, and then you start to reap the benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is an implementation curve and an operationalisation curve before we can reap the benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are infusing AI into teaching, not just as a productivity tool, but in order for us as an Education Service to be able to teach our children what is AI, teach them how to use AI, teach them or enable them to learn with AI, and also to learn beyond AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, all this does requires change management, over and on top of the School Cockpit and suite of tools, AI and tech in nature that enable our teachers to do more with limited time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A number of measures I mentioned earlier have helped to moderate the increase in working hours.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we are at it, we keep at it and continue to roll out reviews and changes that will help to moderate our teachers' overall working hours and their work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling, I know you had a question for tomorrow's Sitting as well.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One, as schools differ in size and profile, how does MOE ensure that requests for additional support staff, such as administrative assistants or counsellors, are prioritised fairly and matched to the unique needs of each school?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Two, are best practices from schools that have successfully reduced teacher workload being shared so that other schools can learn and adopt these methods?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Three, how are insights from these regular workload reviews translated into practical adjustments at the school level, so that teachers feel the impact directly in their day-to-day work?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first, I think I have addressed that in a reply to one of the Members earlier that, based on the specific needs and the profile of each school, if there are additional resource requirements, they can raise them to their superintendents, zonal directors and to HQ, and we will see how to provide support to help them address those needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Certainly, through the Schools Division, our principals, school leaders and our superintendents share best practices, not just in terms of workload reducing measures, but also pedagogical and teaching methods as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have network communities of practice that enable our educators in different fields, as well as our administrators, to be able to share ideas and best practices with one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And lastly, the Member, I believe, asked how we ensure that these measures are properly implemented.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Again, there are a range of supervisory measures, but ultimately, we give our school leaders autonomy and discretion to apply these measures to address needs and circumstances in their institutions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Jackson Lam, did you raise your hand earlier?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I really appreciate the Minister setting the boundaries for clearer parent-teacher communication.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, boundaries can only do so much when it comes to behavioural change.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I am wondering if the Ministry would consider perhaps setting up frameworks to engage parents to set clearer communication guidelines as well as perhaps shared communication platforms, which parents can then engage with should they have concerns about their children?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is because practices may vary between teachers and that might incite some degree of peer influence in terms of responding to parents, especially with their own personal phones for teachers, and parents might have overt concerns about their children, which may also vary between parent groups.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, more than boundaries, my question is whether the Ministry has further measures or frameworks that can be useful to engage parents to enhance this parent-teacher communication?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, parents are the first teachers of our children, and our teachers really work closely and seek to have a close partnership with our parents in order to ensure more holistic education of our children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I mentioned earlier that we have an MOE Engagement Charter, together with the School-Home Partnership framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not just an internal document, it is also shared, particularly with parents as well as with the public, so that we understand how to navigate that relationship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All of us are concerned about our children but we also need to enable our teachers to perform their tasks and to be able to support their children in the class.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And therefore, apart from these two guidelines and frameworks, we also have parent support groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It may vary from school to school, between school leaders, level heads with parents, either en masse, face to face, person to person, in a group, or virtually as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, these are ways that enable a constant relationship, a constant communication between our schools and our parents.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Elysa Chen, I know, like Dr Hamid Razak, you also filed a Parliamentary Question for Thursday's Sitting.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And to follow up, I would like to ask the Minister what safeguards are in place to ensure that internal workload surveys capture the full range of non-teaching duties, including event planning, meetings and administrative work.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And second question: would MOE clarify whether teachers on the teaching track can achieve promotion to General Education Officer 5A and beyond, based solely on classroom teaching excellence, pedagogical innovation and student mentorship, without needing to chair committees or lead school-wide events and nationwide initiatives.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last question: of the teachers promoted to senior teacher or lead teacher positions at the schools, what proportion held non-teaching administrative portfolios, such as committee chairmanships, non-subject Head of Department positions or Year Head roles prior to the appointments, as opposed to solely professional development portfolios?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the second and third question, they are HR- and statistics-related.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would just encourage the Member to file a written Parliamentary Question and we will give her that data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And of course, as with many surveys, there is also a catch-all – that means, anything else, please let us know so that we do not risk missing anything out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And of course, when you average it out, when you then look at it specifically, you then have a very good set of data that enable policy-makers to work.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have already spent an hour and we are only at Question No 5.
